Additive Functions and the Hamel Basis

See how free a function that preserves addition can be. On the rationals it is completely pinned; at irrationals its values come loose.

An additive function obeys f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)f(x + y) = f(x) + f(y)f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y). On the rationals f(q)=qf(1)f(q) = qf(1)f(q)=qf(1) leaves no freedom. But viewing the reals as a vector space over the rationals, 111 and 2\sqrt{2}2​ are independent, so f(2)f(\sqrt{2})f(2​) may be chosen as anything. That freedom is the Hamel basis.

For example, a 📐 square with side 1 has diagonal 2\sqrt{2}2​. Knowing only the side pins nothing about the value assigned to the diagonal, because the diagonal is a new, independent direction. Impose continuity and the freedom vanishes, leaving only a straight line.

f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y),f(q)=qf(1)  (q∈Q)f(x + y) = f(x) + f(y), \qquad f(q) = qf(1) \ \ (q \in \mathbb{Q})f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y),f(q)=qf(1)  (q∈Q)
f(a+b2)=a+bt,t=f(2) is freef(a + b\sqrt{2}) = a + bt, \qquad t = f(\sqrt{2}) \text{ is free}f(a+b2​)=a+bt,t=f(2​) is free

Prove completely that if an additive function fff is continuous at a single point x0x_0x0​, then f(x)=cxf(x) = cxf(x)=cx for every real xxx, where c=f(1)c = f(1)c=f(1).

f additive +continuous at one point ⟹ f(x)=cxf \text{ additive } + \text{continuous at one point} \ \Longrightarrow \ f(x) = cxf additive +continuous at one point ⟹ f(x)=cx
Show proof

  1. Continuity moves to 000: f(x0+h)−f(x0)=f(h)f(x_0 + h) - f(x_0) = f(h)f(x0​+h)−f(x0​)=f(h), so the left side tending to 000 as h→0h \to 0h→0 — continuity at x0x_0x0​ — says exactly f(h)→0=f(0)f(h) \to 0 = f(0)f(h)→0=f(0), continuity at 000. The same identity gives continuity everywhere.
